a16z's Martin Casado on the four mindsets people bring to investing, and why knowing yours stops you from justifying your own bias:

1. Financial

"The correct proxy for the health of a business is the market it's going into and its finances. That's what it is. What are the SaaS metrics? What is the size of the market? That is a proxy for the entire business."

2. Productive

"You believe you're investing in a productive asset, and the productive asset is what's creating value. If you believe in that, as it creates value, it will create market... The type of diligence you do if you're a productive investor is more like, what is the technical approach? What are the adjacent markets?"

3. Frontier

"I think this is the romantic, idealized version of VC from the 60s and 70s, which is kind of YOLO. It's like, founders know better than VCs, and they've seen something that I don't see, and they're gonna go out there and do it. And, like, who am I to second guess them?"

4. Speculative

"It is always so surprising how prevalent it is... They don't even care about the asset. They just want to time a market, right?... They're like, 'Well, this looks cheap. It's clearly gonna go up in value' or, 'This is the top of the market, like, I'm gonna get out.'"

"...You can justify any deal or not justify any deal. So if you don't know what your beliefs are, you'll always basically just kind of justify whatever personal bias you have."

@martin_casado w/ @patrick_oshag on @InvestLikeBest

a16z's Anish Acharya and David Pawlan, creator of Assistant Benchmark, on the gap between people's stated and revealed preferences on privacy, and what that means for AI agent adoption:

"I think in revealed preferences, consumers will share any amount of data for even the most trivial amount of upside."

"People have been connecting their cards, their credit cards, and their bank accounts via Plaid since the Venmo era. But when you ask them, they're like, 'Oh, yes, I'm very concerned about trust and safety.'"

"I think an example though of where consumers are very concerned about sort of trust and assumptions is around being embarrassed and social signaling... The social mechanics actually feel so much higher stakes than the actual, like, real-world implications."

"[One company] offered a million dollars worth of pizza to anyone that wanted to use their product... In order to get that $30 of pizza, you were granting access to your entire Google Workspace, all of your emails, all of your data for 30 bucks."

"It just proves it right there, that people are willing to just give up all that data for some free pizza."

Top-quartile venture beat top-quartile buyout through the internet buildout and again through mobile and cloud, and a16z's Jen Kha argues we're at the start of the next wave.

Tech buyouts have long been the "safe" bet in private markets. Now the stress is showing:

- In the first half of 2026, venture funds marked their tech holdings up 16%, while buyout funds marked theirs down 4%

- 70% of the debt foreclosed in 2025 and 2026 came from deals done in 2021 or 2022

- A typical buyout now needs 10 to 12% EBITDA growth a year to make 2.5x in five years, up from about 5% in 2015

- Top 5% venture funds from 2007-16 returned 5.3x their capital in cash, versus 3.5x for top 5% buyout funds

"Tech buyout is a late-cycle asset class. It's most effective once a technology wave has settled and when business models are predictable enough to borrow against. When a new technology wave drops, all bets are off. By contrast, that's when venture shines."

Full piece from a16z's Jen Kha: https://t.co/FQ7O8OwBe3

Assessing Data Center Risk After a Texas Surprise
While the markets were pricing in a Democratic takeover of both the House and the Senate to some extent, we believe the magnitude of the win was unexpected. Most notably, a new Democratic Governor in Texas was not our base case, we think this introduces new questions and greater uncertainty for many PSPs operating in that region. We believe states with available power and comparatively lower near-term political risk, such as North Dakota, Louisiana and Kentucky, could stand to benefit from a potential moratorium on Texas data centers.

All Eyes on Texas: Texas holds ~30% of data center capacity currently under construction nationally, and Governor-elect Hinojosa has floated a broad moratorium on new sites until new legislation can be put in place. With the scope, mechanism and timeline all undefined, we expect greater uncertainty to continue to drive a risk-off reaction to many Texas based operators. Governor Abbott currently has two months left in office and retains the ability to push project approvals through before handoff, a dynamic that could favor operators who are already energized or sit at the front of ERCOT's interconnection queue.

Key Questions the market is Asking:
Scope and mechanism of a moratorium: Would it cover only new applications or also projects under      construction or with an interconnect agreement in hand?
PUCT Control: With two seats expiring in September 2027, could Hinojosa's appointments change the trajectory of ERCOT into 2028?
Fate of the ERCOT Process: Will ERCOT's interconnection process continue as planned?
Energization dates: Is a reasonable base case that the mega projects with energization dates in proceed as planned?
Grandfathering of executed agreements: For sites planned in 2H27 and beyond, is a signed PPA or interconnection agreement protected from retroactive review or do those publicly committed project timelines still hold if tenants are already secured (such as HUT's Beacon Point Phase 2 project with a signed tenant)?
Sales-tax repeal bill: With the bill already advancing in the Senate under GOP control, will the trajectory change under a Democratic governor?

haha, this is why I seem to have diverged from market's opinion on MSFT. The fact that MSFT only has access to OAI IP till 2032 is a strong argument imo to give MSFT a lower terminal multiple than other hyperscalers, especially given they also have the weakest in-house chip program.

I guess more importantly, the companies in the frontier race may cumulatively spend probably $2 trillion till 2032 on R&D (most of which will be for frontier model training) at least partly because they think RSI will let the leaders compound their lead. If they’re even partly right, 5+ years of leaning on licensed IP could leave Microsoft’s own R&D muscle atrophied. Market clearly doesn't seem too worried, but I personally am which is why I am unwilling to touch MSFT stock anytime soon.
